title: Reverse a Linked List
directAnswer: Walk the list once with three pointers — prev, cur, next. For each node, save cur.next, flip cur.next to point at prev, then slide prev and cur forward. Return prev, which ends on the old tail (the new head). O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Three-pointer in-place reversal: save next, flip, advance
remember.formula:
prev = None
cur = head
while cur:
    nxt = cur.next   # save before we overwrite
    cur.next = prev  # flip the link
    prev = cur       # advance prev
    cur = nxt        # advance cur
return prev
rules: Save `cur.next` into a temp **before** writing `cur.next = prev`, or you lose the rest of the list.
**Return `prev`, not `cur`.** When the loop ends `cur` is null; `prev` is the old tail = new head.
Start `prev = null` so the old head correctly becomes the new tail (its next is null).
Advance in the right order: set `prev = cur` then `cur = nxt` — both use values captured this pass.
Reversal is in-place: you rewire existing nodes, you do not allocate new ones.
whenToUse: Reverse a singly linked list in O(1) extra space
Reverse a sub-segment (Reverse Linked List II) — same loop, bounded range
Reverse in groups of k (Reverse Nodes in k-Group)
Check a palindrome list by reversing the second half
antiSignals: You need the list unchanged → copy it, or use recursion that rebuilds, not in-place flip
It's a doubly linked list → swap prev/next on each node instead of the three-pointer dance
You only need to *print* in reverse → recurse and print on the way back, no rewiring needed
remember.takeaway: Three-pointer reversal is the most-asked linked-list manipulation. The whole trick is 'save next before you flip', and returning prev. Internalise this loop — k-group reversal, palindrome checks, and reorder-list all build on it.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can rewire pointers in place without losing the list, manage the three-pointer bookkeeping, and recognise that the loop ends with prev (not cur) as the new head.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Overwriting cur.next = prev before saving the old next (orphaning the rest of the list), or returning cur/head instead of prev.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State O(n)/O(1), narrate the four-line loop body in order (save, flip, advance prev, advance cur), and mention this is the engine behind k-group reversal and palindrome checks.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list.

Reverse the list so the last node becomes the first, and return **the head of the reversed list**.

The reversal should be done in place — rewire the existing nodes rather than allocating new ones.
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
understanding: Flip the direction of every next pointer. Node values stay where they are; only the links change. After reversal the old tail is the new head and the old head's next becomes null. An empty or single-node list is returned unchanged.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I reverse in place or build a new list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In place is expected — O(1) extra space by rewiring existing next pointers. Building a copy wastes O(n) memory.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What do I return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The new head, which is the old tail. With the iterative method that's the prev pointer after the loop finishes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about an empty or single-node list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return it as-is. The loop handles both: empty → prev stays null; single node → it points at null and is returned.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Iterative or recursive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Iterative is O(1) space and the default. Recursion is elegant but uses O(n) stack — mention both, prefer iterative.

examples.explanation: Every next pointer is flipped; node 5 becomes the head, node 1 the tail.
2 points at 1, 1 points at null. Returned head is 2.
Empty list: the loop never runs, prev stays null, null is returned.

approaches.name: Recursive Reversal
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the elegant alternative, then note it costs O(n) stack space and prefer the iterative version.
hints: If the rest of the list (everything after head) were already reversed, how would you attach the current head onto its end?
Recurse to the end to get the new head. On the way back, make head.next point back at head, and set head.next = null.
Base case: an empty list or a single node is its own reverse — return head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One recursive call per node → O(n) time. The call stack reaches depth n before unwinding → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Recurse all the way to the last node, which becomes the new head and is passed back up unchanged. As each call returns, it fixes the link between the current node and the one after it.

**The base case.** If `head` is null (empty) or `head.next` is null (single node), the list is already its own reverse — return `head`. The single-node case is what stops the recursion and supplies the new head that propagates back up.

**The rewiring on the way back.** Suppose `head` is node A and the recursive call has already reversed everything after it, returning `newHead`. The node directly after A is `head.next`; to flip that link we set `head.next.next = head` (the next node now points back at A), then `head.next = null` (A becomes the tail of whatever precedes it). We return `newHead` unchanged at every level so the original deepest node bubbles up as the final head.

**Why O(n) space.** Each node adds a frame to the call stack, so the stack is n deep at its peak. For n up to 10⁵ that risks a stack overflow — which is exactly why the iterative version is preferred in interviews.
approaches.insight: The recursive version reads as 'reverse the tail, then hook the head onto the back of it'. It's beautiful but the O(n) stack is a real liability on long lists — always be ready to convert it to the O(1) iterative loop.

diagrams.caption: After reaching node 3, each return flips one link back toward the head.

pitfalls: Returning head instead of newHead — head is the old (now last) node, not the new head.
Forgetting head.next = null — leaves a cycle between the last two nodes.
Risking stack overflow on very long lists because the recursion depth is O(n).

edgeCases.behavior: Base case head == null → return null immediately.
Base case head.next == null → return the single node unchanged.

approaches.name: Iterative Three-Pointer Reversal (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — O(1) space. Narrate the loop body: save next, flip link, advance prev, advance cur.
hints: To flip a node's pointer to face backward, you need a handle on the node *behind* it. What pointer tracks that?
Keep three pointers: prev (node behind, starts null), cur (node you're flipping), nxt (saved successor so you don't lose the list).
Each iteration: save nxt = cur.next, set cur.next = prev, then move prev = cur and cur = nxt. When cur is null, prev is the new head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass over n nodes, constant work each → O(n) time. Three pointers regardless of list size → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain three pointers and flip one link per iteration. `prev` is the node we've already reversed up to (starts null), `cur` is the node whose link we're about to flip, and a temporary `nxt` holds `cur.next` so we don't lose the tail when we overwrite it.

**Why save `nxt` first.** The line `cur.next = prev` destroys `cur`'s forward link. If we hadn't stashed it in `nxt` beforehand, the entire remainder of the list would be unreachable — orphaned the instant we overwrite the pointer. So the very first action each pass is `nxt = cur.next`.

**The flip and the slide.** After saving, `cur.next = prev` turns the link backward. Then we advance: `prev = cur` (the node we just finished becomes the new 'behind' marker) and `cur = nxt` (move on to the next node to flip). Both advances use values captured this pass, which is why ordering them as prev-then-cur is safe.

**Why return `prev`.** The loop ends when `cur` becomes null — i.e. we've walked off the end. At that moment `prev` points at the last node we flipped, which is the old tail and therefore the new head. Returning `cur` (null) or the original `head` (now the tail) are the two classic wrong answers.

**Why `prev` starts null.** The old head must become the new tail, and a tail's next is null. Initialising `prev = null` makes the very first flip set `head.next = null` automatically.
approaches.insight: The whole algorithm is four lines that never look more than one node ahead. 'Save next before you flip' is the single idea; everything else is bookkeeping. This exact loop, bounded to a range, is how you reverse a sublist or each k-sized group.

dryRun.intro: prev starts null. Each step: save nxt, flip cur.next = prev, slide prev and cur. Return prev.

code.python:
def reverseList(self, head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur is not None:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev

java.explanation: Node behind cur; starts null so the old head becomes the new tail.
Save the successor BEFORE overwriting cur.next, or the rest of the list is lost.
Flip the link to face backward.
Advance prev to the node we just reversed.
Advance cur to the saved successor.
cur is null now; prev is the old tail = new head.

python.explanation: Behind-pointer; the old head's next will become None.
Stash the next node before we clobber the link.
Slide cur forward to the saved node.
Return the new head — NOT cur (None) or the old head.

diagrams.title: Three pointers flipping links
diagrams.caption: prev trails behind, cur is the node being flipped; the reversed prefix grows left.

pitfalls: Writing cur.next = prev before saving nxt — orphans the rest of the list.
Returning cur (null) or head (old tail) instead of prev.
Initialising prev = head instead of null — creates a self-loop on the first node.
Swapping the advance order so prev = cur runs after cur = nxt — then prev tracks the wrong node.

edgeCases.behavior: cur is null immediately; loop skipped; prev (null) returned → empty list.

commonMistakes: Overwriting cur.next before stashing the next node, losing the rest of the list.
Returning head or cur instead of prev — the new head is prev when the loop ends.
Initialising prev to head instead of null, creating a cycle on the first node.
Using recursion on a 10⁵-node list and overflowing the call stack.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Flipping before saving the next pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: cur.next = prev overwrites the only reference to the rest of the list. Without saving nxt first, every node after cur is orphaned and the loop can't advance.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the wrong pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When the loop ends cur is null and the original head is now the tail. The new head is prev, the last node whose link we flipped.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while cur is not None:
    nxt = cur.next
    cur.next = prev
    prev = cur
    cur = nxt
return head   # head is now the TAIL
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while cur is not None:
    nxt = cur.next
    cur.next = prev
    prev = cur
    cur = nxt
return prev   # prev is the new head
